newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-DFS purchase boosts LVMH H1 sales.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-DFS purchase boosts LVMH H1 sales.

text.p: France's LVMH Moet Hennessy Louis Vuitton on Wednesday reported a surge in half-year sales after the contribution of its U.S. acquisition Duty Free Shoppers.

The French luxury goods flagship, whose brands range from Moet & Chandon champagne to Kenzo, Guerlain and Christian Dior, said sales jumped 62 percent to 21.59 billion francs ($3.4 billion) for the six months to June 30 from 13.37 billion for the year-earlier period.
At a constant structure, sales were up 9.4 percent, it said in a statement.
LVMH's stock tumbled, however, on disappointment with the performance of the cognac business and the upscale DFS chain.
The shares were down 2.69 percent at 1,482 francs in late trade, while the Paris bourse's CAC-40 index was 1.6 percent lower.
Analysts said they were told in a conference call with LVMH that cognac sales fell 20 percent in Japan, which accounts for around a quarter of LVMH's cognac business.
The drop was partly offset by a 10 percent rise in U.S. cognac volumes, but cognac and spirits sales overall fell to 2.34 billion francs in the first half from 2.36 billion a year earlier.

DFS sales, measured in dollars, fell 10 percent largely because of the yen's weakness, analysts said. But the dollar's strength meant the revenue was two percent higher when translated into French francs.
Although the cognac and DFS results were disappointing, they did not come as a surprise, analysts said.
"I think LVMH is penalised more by the lack of visibility on the Guinness and Grand Metropolitan affair than on the sales results," one analyst said of the stock's drop.

After building up an 11.06 percent stake in GrandMet, LVMH appears to have paused in its drive to force the British companies to drop their 24 billion pound merger plan and agree to a three-way drinks deal.
A source close to the French company said further developments in the saga were not expected before the end of the month, after the French summer holidays.

Sales of LVMH perfumes, including Christian Dior's Dolce Vita and Dune, rose six percent in a half-year increase capped by the group's continuing efforts to keep its products from being channelled into the parallel market and ending up on discounters' shelves.
Louis Vuitton baggage sales rose 22 percent, leading the advance in the leather goods branch, the business with the biggest profit margin for LVMH, to 5.71 billion francs in sales from 4.76 billion.
"It wasn't all bad news," one analyst said, adding that the dollar's strength bodes well for future results. "That will kick in later," he said.
LVMH's acquisition in January of majority control of San Francisco-based DFS for $2.6 billion will hugely increase its sales in dollars and dollar-linked currencies.
Chairman Bernard Arnault cautioned in May that DFS's results would be inferior to last year's because of the yen's weakness.
The company said in January that the DFS acquisition would boost cashflow and pre-exceptional profit before goodwill amortisation but cut earnings per share for 1997.
